planting.note: Grow as a climbing terrarium or greenhouse subject on a damp mossy pole or bark slab, since this Central American species roots along its stem between leaf nodes as it climbs and needs constant contact with a humid surface to do so. Keep the chunky, bark-based mix evenly moist but never waterlogged, and provide bright, filtered light rather than direct sun. All parts are toxic if ingested.

directions: Anthurium flexile is a vining, hemiepiphytic aroid native to wet lowland and lower-montane forests from southern Mexico through Central America to Panama, where it climbs tree trunks using narrow, elongated, semiglossy leaves and roots that anchor directly into the bark at each node. It is one of only a small handful of Central American Anthurium species with this climbing, stem-rooting habit, which also distinguishes the better-known South American species A. clidemioides, and it remains relatively rare in cultivation compared to showier flowering or velvet-leaf anthuriums. The green, lance-shaped spathe and violet-purple spadix are modest compared to ornamental hybrids, so the plant is grown mainly for its climbing foliage habit in terrarium, vivarium, or warm greenhouse settings where humidity stays consistently high. Provide a mossy or bark climbing support early, keep nights above 60F, and avoid letting the mix dry out completely, since the fine roots that anchor it to its support are easily damaged by drought stress.

planting.note: Grow year-round as an indoor foliage plant in bright, indirect light; move to a shaded porch or patio in summer once nights stay reliably above 55F. Give it more floor space than the dwarf Jubilee Compact sport, since the standard form builds a larger, fuller clump over time.

directions: Jubilee is a Chinese evergreen hybrid bred by B. Frank Brown in 1984 from a cross of Aglaonema nitidum f. curtisii as the seed parent with Aglaonema hybrida 'Manilla,' and it is the full-size parent behind the later, more compact Jubilee Compact sport grown for the same leaf pattern on a smaller plant. Its thick, leathery, ovate leaves carry a dark green base overlaid with a silver-green center and irregular chevron-shaped silver markings that radiate outward along the veins, giving a bolder, more dramatic look than plain green aglaonemas. The plant builds a dense, upright, freely branching clump considerably larger than its dwarf sport, eventually reaching roughly two to two and a half feet tall and wide where the Compact form stays noticeably shorter. Keep it in low to bright indirect light away from direct sun, let the top inch of soil dry between waterings, and protect it from temperatures below 55F, since cold quickly causes chilling injury and leaf spotting in this tropical foliage hybrid.
